messages.content: I want to develop a learned plasma fluid closure that recovers collisionless plasma echoes while preserving energy under unseen forcing histories. The targets are to predict echo amplitudes within 10% of Vlasov–Poisson reference values on held-out forcing histories and to keep unforced total energy drift below 0.1% over 100 plasma periods.

That sets two distinct requirements for the closure. Its echo-amplitude predictions need to be close to the Vlasov–Poisson reference on forcing histories held out from learning. Separately, when the system is unforced, its total energy must drift by less than 0.1% over 100 plasma periods. Those are development targets, not claims that a closure has already met them.
Why emphasize collisionless plasma echoes rather than just saying the closure should predict the plasma response?

Because the echo is the particular response the goal asks the learned fluid closure to recover. A closure might describe some aspects of a plasma response yet fail to reproduce the echo amplitude accurately. Naming collisionless echoes keeps that requirement explicit rather than letting a broader description of response stand in for it.
And what work is the phrase “held-out forcing histories” doing?

It makes the echo-amplitude target a test on forcing histories not used in learning. The requirement is not merely to match the histories the closure has already encountered. The node does not specify what those histories look like or how they are selected; it specifies the held-out condition for the comparison.
Is the Vlasov–Poisson result the comparison point for both targets?

It is explicitly the reference for the echo amplitudes: predictions should be within 10% of the corresponding Vlasov–Poisson reference values on held-out forcing histories. The energy requirement is stated separately as a limit on unforced total energy drift. It does not explicitly define that drift as an error against a Vlasov–Poisson energy trace.
So I should not describe the energy target as another 10% comparison?

Right. The numbers apply to different quantities and conditions. The 10% threshold concerns echo amplitudes relative to Vlasov–Poisson reference values under held-out forcing histories. The energy threshold is below 0.1% drift in unforced total energy over 100 plasma periods.
Does “preserving energy” here mean exact energy conservation?

The stated quantitative requirement is not exact conservation. It allows some unforced total energy drift, provided that drift remains below 0.1% over 100 plasma periods. “Preserving energy” describes the aim; the drift limit gives its stated acceptance threshold.
How should I think about the forced and unforced conditions together?

They serve different parts of the goal. Unseen, held-out forcing histories are where echo amplitudes are compared with the Vlasov–Poisson references. The energy-drift limit is expressly for the unforced case. Nothing in these requirements assigns that same unforced drift limit to periods when forcing is applied.
Could I say that accurate echoes alone establish success?

Not for this goal. Echo amplitudes within 10% of the reference on held-out forcing histories would address one requirement, while unforced total energy drift below 0.1% over 100 plasma periods addresses the other. The closure is meant to satisfy both.
Likewise, a closure with low unforced energy drift might still miss the main echo objective?
Yes. Low drift by itself would not show that the closure recovers collisionless plasma echoes. The echo-amplitude comparison is a separate, explicit measure of that part of the objective.
Does “learned plasma fluid closure” specify a particular model or learning procedure?

No particular architecture, training procedure, or closure formula is specified. The phrase identifies the kind of object to develop: a learned closure for a plasma fluid description. The stated requirements concern what that closure should reproduce and how its energy behavior should be bounded, not a prescribed implementation.
Would it be fair to interpret “unseen forcing histories” as a demand for generalization, without claiming which kinds of forcing it will generalize to?

Yes. The held-out condition means the echo-amplitude target must be met on histories not seen during learning. It does not, by itself, identify particular forcing patterns or establish performance on every possible forcing history.
What exactly is being compared when we say “within 10%”?

The quantities named are echo amplitudes predicted by the learned closure and echo amplitudes in the Vlasov–Poisson reference, evaluated on held-out forcing histories. “Within 10%” states the intended closeness of those amplitudes. The node does not give a more detailed scoring convention or a method for extracting an amplitude.
Should the 100 plasma periods be attached to the echo prediction too?

No. The duration of 100 plasma periods belongs to the unforced total-energy-drift requirement. The echo-amplitude requirement specifies held-out forcing histories and the 10% comparison with Vlasov–Poisson reference values, but it does not state that same duration for the echo comparison.
I also don't want the wording to imply that energy was measured under those held-out forcing histories.

Then keep the conditions explicit: echo amplitudes are judged on held-out forcing histories, while total energy drift is bounded in the unforced case. That preserves the distinction without implying a forced-energy result that the goal does not state.
Does the goal say anything about other conserved quantities or about matching the full Vlasov–Poisson solution?

It does not state requirements for other conserved quantities or for agreement with the full Vlasov–Poisson solution. The specified reference comparison is for echo amplitudes, and the specified preservation criterion is for unforced total energy over 100 plasma periods.
Then the central challenge is meeting an echo-fidelity target without sacrificing the stated energy behavior?

That captures the combined aim without presuming a particular trade-off or mechanism. The learned plasma fluid closure should recover collisionless plasma echoes to the stated amplitude tolerance on held-out forcing histories and keep unforced total energy drift below the stated limit. Whether or how those demands interact is not specified.
Can you give me one compact formulation that retains both conditions?

Develop a learned plasma fluid closure that predicts collisionless plasma echo amplitudes within 10% of Vlasov–Poisson reference values on held-out forcing histories, while keeping unforced total energy drift below 0.1% over 100 plasma periods.
And that remains a target, not a reported result?
Yes. It states what the closure is intended to achieve; it does not say that a closure has been built or that either threshold has been demonstrated.

For the learned closure, I propose training a skew-symmetric Hamiltonian fluid closure with Fourier–Hermite memory modes. The idea is to use the memory modes for echo recovery and the Hamiltonian structure for exact unforced energy conservation.

That is a proposed approach, not a reported result. It combines a learned fluid closure with two intended features: Fourier–Hermite memory modes to support recovery of collisionless plasma echoes, and a skew-symmetric Hamiltonian structure intended to conserve energy exactly when the system is unforced. The proposal does not yet establish that either feature achieves its aim.
Why include memory modes at all?

Their stated role in the proposal is echo recovery. Calling them memory modes emphasizes that the closure is meant to retain information relevant to a response that cannot simply be described as an instantaneous fluid state. That explains the motivation without claiming that the proposed modes have already reproduced an echo.
Does “Fourier–Hermite” tell us how many memory modes to train?
No. It identifies the proposed modal form, but the proposal gives no mode count, truncation, or training specification. Those details should not be inferred from the name.
What does skew symmetry contribute to the energy-conservation idea?

In a general Hamiltonian illustration, suppose an unforced state z evolves as dz/dt = J(z)∇H(z), where H is an energy and J is skew-symmetric. If H has no explicit time dependence, then dH/dt = ∇H·J∇H = 0, because a vector contracted with a skew-symmetric operator in that way gives zero. This illustrates why skew symmetry is relevant to exact unforced conservation; it does not prove that a particular trained closure or numerical implementation has it.
So “Hamiltonian” and “skew-symmetric” are not just two unrelated labels?

They are connected in the proposed structure. Skew symmetry supplies the cancellation in the idealized energy argument, while “Hamiltonian” frames the evolution in terms of an energy and its associated dynamics. The proposal names that structural approach without supplying a specific Hamiltonian, operator, or closure equation.
Does exact unforced energy conservation mean the forcing histories must conserve energy too?

No. The word “unforced” limits the conservation claim being sought. The proposal does not say that total energy stays constant while forcing is applied, nor does it specify an energy balance for the forced case. Forced histories remain relevant to assessing echo recovery, but they are not covered by a claim of unforced conservation.
Would the skew-symmetric structure automatically make the echoes accurate?

No such implication is stated. The proposal assigns echo recovery to the closure with its Fourier–Hermite memory modes and exact unforced energy conservation to the skew-symmetric Hamiltonian structure. Meeting one aim would not, by itself, demonstrate the other.
Could the memory modes interfere with the intended energy conservation?

The proposal does not specify how those modes are coupled to the rest of the fluid closure, so it does not settle that question. For the intended exact unforced conservation to hold, the complete unforced dynamics—including whatever role the memory modes play—would have to respect the relevant energy-conserving structure. Merely naming a skew-symmetric component would not establish conservation for an otherwise unspecified full model.
Am I claiming a proof when I say “exact unforced energy conservation”?

Not as this proposal is worded. It states an intended property of the closure to be trained, rather than presenting a proof or an observed result. It is worth retaining “exact,” because that is the property proposed, while keeping clear that the property has not been demonstrated here.
Is there also a distinction between a conservation property of the equations and one observed in computed trajectories?

Yes. An ideal unforced evolution can have an exact energy identity, while a numerical realization does not automatically preserve that identity exactly. The proposal does not specify numerical discretization or establish exact conservation in computed trajectories, so its structural intention should not be turned into a numerical performance claim.
How does this relate to the echo and energy criteria we discussed?

It proposes a way to pursue both kinds of behavior: the Fourier–Hermite memory modes are for echo recovery, and the skew-symmetric Hamiltonian construction is for exact unforced energy conservation. It does not say that echo predictions satisfy the stated Vlasov–Poisson comparison or that an energy-drift criterion has been measured. Those remain criteria for the intended closure, not outcomes established by the proposal.
Would you describe this as a particular trained model already in hand?

No. “Train” describes the proposed activity, and the sentence identifies the kind of closure to train. It gives neither a completed model nor training results, parameter choices, or test measurements.
Can you restate the proposal without adding a training recipe?

Train a skew-symmetric Hamiltonian plasma fluid closure with Fourier–Hermite memory modes, using those modes to pursue collisionless echo recovery and the proposed structure to pursue exact energy conservation in the unforced case. That states the approach and its intended outcomes without implying that either has already been achieved.
How many Hermite memory modes preserve echo amplitudes within 10% across unseen two-pulse delays of 10–40 plasma periods?

There is no mode count in the information given. The question asks which Hermite memory-mode count, if any, achieves the 10% echo-amplitude tolerance on unseen two-pulse delays spanning 10–40 plasma periods. Answering it with a number would require results for candidate counts on those held-out delays.
Does the 10–40 plasma-period range let us work out a count theoretically?

Not by itself. It specifies the range of delays over which the echo-amplitude requirement is being asked about; it is not a formula for the number of Hermite memory modes. The question gives no relationship that converts delay into a sufficient mode count.
What exactly is the delay here?

In “two-pulse delays,” the delay is the separation between the two pulses, expressed in plasma periods. The question specifies separations from 10 to 40 plasma periods. It does not specify pulse shapes, strengths, or a particular list of delays within that range.
Why say “unseen” rather than simply “two-pulse delays”?

“Unseen” makes the question about performance beyond the histories used to learn the closure. A mode count would not answer this question merely because it gave close echo amplitudes for two-pulse delays already encountered during learning; the stated test concerns unseen delays in the 10–40-plasma-period range.
When we say the amplitudes are within 10%, what are they within 10% of?

The stated echo-amplitude reference for the closure is Vlasov–Poisson. Here the relevant comparison is between the closure’s predicted echo amplitudes and the Vlasov–Poisson reference amplitudes for the unseen two-pulse delays. The question does not supply those amplitudes or report any comparisons.
Is this asking for the smallest number of modes that works?

It asks “how many,” but does not explicitly say “the smallest number.” One could use the question to seek a sufficient count, or distinguish the smallest count that meets the tolerance if results across counts were available. Neither a sufficient count nor a minimum can be identified from the information provided.
Could we at least say that more Hermite modes will always improve the echo-amplitude match?

No. The question supplies no results showing how echo-amplitude error changes with mode count, so it does not establish monotonic improvement. More modes might change the prediction, but a claim that they always improve this particular comparison would go beyond what is known here.
Does “across unseen two-pulse delays of 10–40 plasma periods” mean that one successful delay is enough?

No; “across” asks about performance over the stated delay range, not just at one chosen delay. The wording does not specify an exact list of held-out delays or a scoring rule for aggregating them, so it should not be turned into a claim that one successful comparison settles the question.
Could a result at a 10-plasma-period delay settle what happens at a 40-plasma-period delay?

Not on the information given. Both delays fall within the range named in the question, but performance at one does not establish performance at the other. The point of asking about delays from 10 to 40 plasma periods is to address the echo-amplitude tolerance over that range.
And a good average over delays might conceal a delay that misses 10%, depending on how the requirement is read?

Yes. An average error and a requirement that amplitudes remain within 10% throughout the tested range are different interpretations. The question says “within 10% across” the unseen delays but does not define an aggregation statistic. An answer should make clear which interpretation its evidence supports rather than silently substituting one for the other.
Does the proposed Hamiltonian structure answer the mode-count question indirectly, because it is intended to conserve energy?

No. Exact unforced energy conservation is an intended structural property of the proposed closure; it does not specify how many Hermite memory modes yield echo amplitudes within 10% of Vlasov–Poisson values at unseen two-pulse delays. Energy behavior and this echo-amplitude question are distinct.
Should I take “preserve echo amplitudes” to mean the modes themselves each carry a fixed fraction of an echo?

The question does not assign an amplitude contribution to any individual mode. “Preserve echo amplitudes within 10%” describes the accuracy sought from the closure at a given mode count. It does not provide a per-mode decomposition or a way to calculate the count from individual contributions.
Can I answer with a plausible numerical guess, provided I label it as a guess?

A labeled guess would still not answer which count meets the stated tolerance. No measured amplitudes or mode-count comparisons have been provided, so there is no basis here for a specific numerical count—even a tentative one.
What would distinguish an actual answer from just repeating the question?

An actual answer would identify a Hermite memory-mode count and support its claimed echo-amplitude accuracy against the Vlasov–Poisson reference on unseen two-pulse delays in the 10–40-plasma-period range. If the intent is to identify a minimum, it would also need support for why fewer modes do not meet that same criterion. None of those results is supplied in the question.
So how should I phrase the answer for now without implying that a count has been found?

The number of Hermite memory modes needed is undetermined. The open question is which count can keep predicted echo amplitudes within 10% of Vlasov–Poisson reference values across unseen two-pulse delays of 10–40 plasma periods.
Here is my hypothesis about the mode count: at kλ_D=0.1, 256 Hermite modes achieve ≤10% echo-amplitude error for held-out two-pulse delays of 10–40 plasma periods, while 32 modes do not.

That is a specific, testable hypothesis. It identifies the setting, kλ_D=0.1; the two mode counts, 256 and 32; the held-out two-pulse delay range, 10–40 plasma periods; and the echo-amplitude threshold, ≤10%. It predicts that 256 modes meet the threshold across those delays and that 32 modes fail to meet it. It does not report a result.
What does specifying kλ_D=0.1 add?

It confines the prediction to that stated value of kλ_D. The hypothesis does not say that the same mode-count comparison holds at other values. Here kλ_D is the dimensionless product of a wavenumber k and the Debye length λ_D; no further parameter values are given.
Should I say 256 modes are sufficient in general?

Not on the strength of this hypothesis. The proposed sufficiency is for ≤10% echo-amplitude error at kλ_D=0.1 on held-out two-pulse delays of 10–40 plasma periods. “Sufficient in general” would extend the claim beyond those conditions.
Does this give an answer to how many modes are needed?

It proposes an answer under the specified conditions: 256 modes meet the stated tolerance, and 32 do not. Because it is a hypothesis rather than an established result, it cannot yet be stated as a demonstrated answer. It also does not identify the smallest count that could work.
Why doesn't comparing 32 and 256 establish 256 as the minimum?

The hypothesis says nothing about counts between 32 and 256. Some intermediate count could meet the threshold, or none could; the statement does not decide that. It distinguishes the two named counts without locating a minimum.
Could I infer that every count below 256 fails?

No. The failure prediction is specifically for 32 modes. It does not make a prediction for every smaller count or for all counts below 256, and it does not state that echo-amplitude accuracy changes monotonically with mode count.
When I say that 32 modes do not meet the threshold, am I saying their error exceeds 10% at every delay?

Not necessarily. The hypothesis says 32 modes do not achieve the ≤10% criterion across the held-out 10–40-plasma-period delay range. It does not give errors at individual delays or say that every delay exceeds 10%. That stronger claim should not be added.
Similarly, does the hypothesis give an exact error for 256 modes?

No. It predicts that the echo-amplitude error is at most 10% under the stated held-out-delay condition. It does not say whether the error is exactly 10%, much smaller, or different from one delay to another.
Is an error of exactly 10% permitted by the wording?

Yes. The symbol ≤ includes equality: an error of exactly 10% satisfies that part of the hypothesis. An error greater than 10% would not satisfy it under the applicable interpretation of the delay-range criterion.
What are the predicted echo amplitudes being compared with?

The established comparison for echo-amplitude accuracy is to Vlasov–Poisson reference values. In this hypothesis, the proposed ≤10% error concerns echo amplitudes at the specified kλ_D value and held-out two-pulse delays. No reference amplitudes or calculated errors are supplied here.
Why keep the word “held-out” in the hypothesis?

Because the prediction concerns delays not used in learning, rather than merely reproducing echo amplitudes for histories the closure has already encountered. Removing “held-out” would weaken an explicit condition of the hypothesis.
Does “10–40 plasma periods” mean the length of the energy-conservation test?

No. In this hypothesis, 10–40 plasma periods specifies the range of delays between the two pulses for the echo-amplitude comparison. It is not an energy-drift duration, and this hypothesis makes no energy-conservation prediction.
Is the 256-versus-32 comparison itself evidence that the memory modes recover echoes?

Not yet. It is a predicted contrast in echo-amplitude accuracy between two Hermite mode counts. Evidence would require the corresponding held-out comparisons; the hypothesis alone does not establish either predicted outcome.
Could I describe 32 modes as producing no echo?

No. Failing a ≤10% echo-amplitude-error threshold does not mean an echo is absent. The hypothesis predicts only that 32 modes do not meet that accuracy criterion across the specified delays; it says nothing about whether an echo is present or what its amplitude is.
And 256 modes meeting the amplitude threshold would not necessarily mean every aspect of the echo matches?
Correct. The prediction is specifically about echo-amplitude error. It does not assert agreement in every feature of the response or in the full Vlasov–Poisson solution.
Does this hypothesis prescribe how to train the closure or choose the held-out delays?

No. It names the mode counts, the value kλ_D=0.1, the held-out two-pulse delay range, and the predicted error outcomes. It gives no training procedure, list of delays, or detailed error-aggregation rule.
How can we keep the uncertainty clear in a short restatement?

Use predictive language: “We hypothesize that, at kλ_D=0.1, 256 Hermite modes achieve ≤10% echo-amplitude error on held-out two-pulse delays of 10–40 plasma periods, whereas 32 modes do not.” That preserves the comparison and conditions without presenting either outcome as observed.
So the precise claim is about those two counts at that parameter value and delay range, not a universal rule for Hermite modes?

Exactly. The hypothesis contrasts 256 and 32 Hermite modes for echo-amplitude accuracy at kλ_D=0.1 on held-out two-pulse delays of 10–40 plasma periods. It does not establish a universal mode-count rule or a minimum sufficient count.

I plan to train 32-, 64-, 128-, and 256-mode closures at kλ_D=0.1, then compare their echo errors across held-out two-pulse delays of 10–40 plasma periods and their unforced energy drift over 100 plasma periods.

That lays out a comparison across four mode counts under the same stated value, kλ_D=0.1. The echo comparison concerns held-out two-pulse delays ranging from 10 to 40 plasma periods; the energy comparison concerns unforced drift over 100 plasma periods. It is a plan for training and comparison, not a report of results.
What question does including all four mode counts help address?

It helps investigate how the number of modes relates to echo-amplitude accuracy over the stated held-out delay range. Comparing 32, 64, 128, and 256 modes can distinguish their observed behavior if results become available. Listing those counts does not itself show which count meets the echo-error target.
Why look at energy drift in the same plan if the mode-count question is about echoes?

The closure is intended to recover echoes while preserving energy. Including unforced 100-plasma-period energy drift keeps the energy behavior visible alongside the echo errors for the proposed mode counts. It does not assume that a closure with a smaller echo error also has a smaller energy drift, or vice versa.
Does the plan call for energy drift to be measured during the two-pulse forcing?

No. It specifies echo errors across held-out two-pulse delays and, separately, unforced energy drift over 100 plasma periods. The word “unforced” matters: the plan does not state a forced-case energy-drift comparison.
And are the 10–40 periods and the 100 periods describing the same interval?

No. The 10–40-plasma-period range describes delays between the two pulses in the held-out echo comparisons. The 100 plasma periods describe the duration over which unforced energy drift is compared. They are different conditions attached to different quantities.
Does “held-out” apply to both comparisons?

The plan explicitly attaches held-out status to the delays used for the echo-error comparison. It does not specify a corresponding held-out-history condition for the unforced energy-drift comparison. That distinction is worth preserving rather than silently extending the wording.
What would “compare echo errors” mean relative to the stated goal?

The goal uses Vlasov–Poisson reference values for echo amplitudes, with a target of predictions within 10% on held-out forcing histories. In this plan, the relevant echo-error comparison is across the held-out two-pulse delays at kλ_D=0.1. The plan does not provide calculated errors or a detailed rule for combining errors across delays.
Does comparing four counts guarantee that we'll identify the minimum count needed?

No. The planned counts are 32, 64, 128, and 256. Even if their results were known, the plan would directly compare only those four counts; it does not include every possible count between them. It can inform the mode-count question without, by itself, establishing an absolute minimum.
Should I assume echo error falls steadily as we move from 32 to 256 modes?

No trend is specified in the plan. The point of comparing the four closures is to find out how their echo errors behave. A steady improvement with increasing mode count would be a possible observation, not something this plan has already established.
Does the plan say how the training will be done?

It says to train closures at the four listed mode counts and at kλ_D=0.1. It does not specify a training method, data allocation, loss function, or other implementation details. Adding any of those would turn this into a more detailed plan than the one stated.
What about the exact delays within 10–40 plasma periods?

The plan gives the range for the held-out two-pulse delays, not a list of individual delay values or a sampling schedule. Any claim about which specific delays are included would need information beyond the plan.
Could I describe the echo comparison as testing unseen forcing histories?

Yes, provided you keep the form of the histories explicit: the plan concerns held-out two-pulse delays of 10–40 plasma periods. “Unseen forcing histories” captures the held-out aspect, but on its own it would omit the particular two-pulse delay range named here.
Does measuring unforced energy drift establish exact conservation?

Not merely by being in the plan. The comparison would concern observed unforced energy drift over 100 plasma periods, while exact conservation is a stronger structural claim. Neither a drift value nor a proof of exact conservation is supplied here.
How does the energy comparison relate to the numerical target without assuming an outcome?

The stated energy target is unforced total energy drift below 0.1% over 100 plasma periods. The plan calls for comparing unforced 100-period energy drift for the four closures, which would provide information relevant to that target. It does not say that any of the closures stays below 0.1%.
If one mode count had good echo accuracy but poor energy behavior, would the plan still let us see that distinction?

In principle, comparing both quantities for the planned closures would keep those outcomes separate. Echo error across held-out delays and unforced energy drift over 100 plasma periods should not be treated as interchangeable. The plan does not predict such a split or give results for any count.
Can you state the plan compactly without making it sound as though the comparisons have happened?
Train 32-, 64-, 128-, and 256-mode closures at kλ_D=0.1, then compare their echo errors on held-out two-pulse delays of 10–40 plasma periods and their unforced energy drift over 100 plasma periods.
Run VP-Echo40: train four Hermite-mode closures at kλ_D=0.1, then measure their held-out echo errors and their unforced energy drift over 100 plasma periods.

VP-Echo40 calls for training four Hermite-mode closures at kλ_D=0.1 and measuring two outcomes for them: echo errors on held-out cases and unforced energy drift over 100 plasma periods. This states the activity to carry out; it does not provide training outputs or measurements, so I cannot report numerical results from it.
Which four closures does that refer to?
The four mode counts specified for this comparison are 32, 64, 128, and 256 Hermite modes. Each is a closure to be trained at kλ_D=0.1. VP-Echo40 does not state how any of them performs.
Should I treat VP-Echo40 as the name of a result?

No. Here VP-Echo40 names the activity: train the four closures and measure the stated outcomes. The name alone does not imply that a run has finished or that an echo-error or energy-drift value is available.
What is held out in the echo measurement?

The echo errors are to be measured on held-out cases. In the specified comparison, these are two-pulse delays of 10–40 plasma periods that were not used in learning. The activity does not list individual delay values or report errors at any of them.
And what is the echo error measured against?

The echo-amplitude comparison uses Vlasov–Poisson reference values. VP-Echo40 calls for measuring the held-out echo errors of the trained closures; it supplies neither the predicted amplitudes nor the reference amplitudes from which numerical errors could be reported.
Is kλ_D=0.1 a setting for all four mode counts?
Yes. The activity specifies training the four Hermite-mode closures at kλ_D=0.1. It does not describe runs at other values of kλ_D.
How should the two measurements be kept distinct?

The echo measurement concerns error on held-out two-pulse cases. The energy measurement concerns drift in the unforced case over 100 plasma periods. The 10–40-plasma-period range describes the two-pulse delays, whereas 100 plasma periods is the duration of the unforced energy measurement.
Does VP-Echo40 ask for energy drift during the held-out two-pulse cases as well?
No. Its stated energy measurement is 100-period unforced energy drift. It does not specify an energy-drift measurement while the two-pulse forcing is applied.
When it says energy drift, is that the total-energy quantity from the goal?
Yes. The unforced energy criterion concerns total energy, and the activity measures unforced energy drift over the same 100-plasma-period duration. The activity does not give a drift value.
Can you tell me now whether any closure is within 10% on echoes?

No measured held-out echo errors are provided, so I cannot say whether any of the four closures is within 10% of its Vlasov–Poisson reference echo amplitudes. That is one of the outcomes VP-Echo40 is meant to measure.
Can you tell me whether unforced drift is below 0.1%?
Not without the unforced 100-plasma-period measurements. The target is drift below 0.1%, but naming that target does not establish the measured drift of any closure.
If we measure a small drift, does the activity itself prove exact unforced conservation?

No. VP-Echo40 specifies a measurement over 100 plasma periods. A measured drift and a proof of exact conservation are different things; the activity description provides neither a drift result nor such a proof.
Does training the four closures count as measuring their echo errors?

No. Training and measurement are separate parts of the activity. The instruction is to train the closures and then assess their held-out echo errors; training alone would not supply those held-out error values.
Would a training-set echo match be enough to complete the echo part?
No. The requested measurement is of held-out echo errors. A match on cases encountered during learning would not, by itself, provide the held-out measurement specified for VP-Echo40.
Does the activity say which count will have the lowest error?
It does not. It identifies four closures to train and quantities to measure, without ranking their echo errors or energy drift. Any ranking would require the measurements.
Could I call the four-count comparison a search for a mode count that meets the echo tolerance?

Yes, as a description of its purpose: measuring held-out echo errors for the four counts can inform which of those counts, if any, meets the 10% amplitude-error target under the specified conditions. VP-Echo40 itself does not identify a successful count or establish a minimum across all possible counts.
What should a status statement say before the measurements exist?

It can say: “VP-Echo40 is the activity to train 32-, 64-, 128-, and 256-Hermite-mode closures at kλ_D=0.1 and measure held-out echo errors and unforced total-energy drift over 100 plasma periods.” It should not attach performance numbers or claim that the measurements have been completed.
So the word “run” is an instruction here, not evidence that a run took place?
Exactly. “Run VP-Echo40” directs the training and measurements. Without execution records or measured values, it remains an activity to carry out rather than a reported experimental outcome.
The artifact is a VP-Echo40 report with four trained closure checkpoints, held-out echo-amplitude errors, and 100-period unforced energy-drift traces. What does that description tell us?

It identifies what the report contains: four trained closure checkpoints, errors for echo amplitudes on held-out cases, and traces of unforced energy drift spanning 100 plasma periods. It does not give the numerical errors or drift values, so the description alone does not establish whether any closure meets the echo or energy targets.
What is the difference between the checkpoints and the measurements?

The checkpoints are saved trained closures. The held-out echo-amplitude errors and unforced energy-drift traces are measurements associated with evaluating them. A checkpoint identifies a trained closure; it is not itself an echo-error value or an energy-drift trace.
Can we identify which four closures the checkpoints represent?

In the VP-Echo40 comparison, they are the 32-, 64-, 128-, and 256-Hermite-mode closures at kλ_D=0.1. The artifact description says there are four trained checkpoints, but gives no checkpoint-specific performance numbers.
Does the presence of trained checkpoints mean the report contains a complete account of how training was done?
No. The stated contents include the checkpoints, echo-amplitude errors, and energy-drift traces. They do not specify a training recipe or say what additional documentation the report provides.
What does “held-out” qualify in this artifact?

It qualifies the echo-amplitude errors: those errors concern cases held out from learning. The VP-Echo40 comparison concerns two-pulse delays of 10–40 plasma periods. The artifact description does not say that the unforced energy-drift traces are from held-out forcing histories.
Are the echo errors and energy traces measurements of the same condition?

No. The echo-amplitude errors concern held-out two-pulse cases, while the energy-drift traces concern unforced evolution over 100 plasma periods. The report brings both measurements together, but their conditions remain distinct.
Why call the energy information a trace rather than just an energy-drift number?

A trace describes how the measured quantity behaves over the stated interval, whereas a single number would summarize it in some way. The artifact specifically names 100-period unforced energy-drift traces. It does not state their shape, sampling, or any summary drift value.
Could I conclude from those traces that energy was conserved exactly?
